title: Teach Microduck to score a goal
text: What you will build  The final scene contains one Microduck, one football, and one goal. The robot must find the ball, locate the goal, approach a useful kicking position, make contact, and recover its stance. You will learn what each part of this system does and how the parts work together.    1 Understand the mechanism   2 Control and train   3 See and navigate   4 Score autonomously      Play demonstration   A complete task in synchronized robot and external views. Playback follows simulation time. This successful example alone is not a success-rate measurement.     By the end, you can   Explain how joints, actuators, observations, actions, and rewards relate.  Launch a Newton / Isaac Lab simulation and inspect a fixed policy in action.  Run a bounded training exercise, locate checkpoints, and interpret training curves.  Connect camera detections, ToF ranges, and body attitude to autonomous task states.  Record both successes and failures, distinguishing model metrics from task metrics.     Course route      Chapter  The question you will answer      1 · Meet the robot  Which parts move, and what does software control?    2 · Your first simulation  How do you launch a scene and apply a fixed policy?    3 · Learning to walk  How do rewards shape a policy, and where is training saved?    4 · From actions to skills  Why is motion different from completing a skill?    5 · Seeing the ball  How does an image box become useful spatial information?    6 · Navigation and alignment  Why can’t the robot kick as soon as it sees the ball?    7 · Autonomous shooting  How do you connect the modules and judge the whole task?       Choose your learning path →

title: How to take this course
text: Choose a learning path      Path  What you do  What you need      Observe  Read, inspect the 3D assembly, play GIFs, and answer checks.  A modern browser    Use fixed models (recommended)  Copy terminal commands, run simulation, and record observations.  A prepared GPU environment    Practice training  Add your own training, export, and evaluation.  Additional runtime and disk space      For a first pass, complete the fixed-model path, then return to Chapters 3 and 5 for training. Without a GPU, follow the reading path in order. The interactive model and examples do not launch Isaac.    Prerequisites   Open a Linux terminal, change directories, and copy multiline commands.  Read basic Python functions, arrays, and parameters. Prior PPO knowledge is not required.  Understand positions, angles, and velocities; robot coordinate frames are introduced in the course.    About your training results  Your checkpoint is a practice artifact. Later chapters explicitly use the course models in  models/ ; they never select the latest training run automatically. Using your own policy requires an explicit checkpoint and a new evaluation.     A useful lab routine   Read the expected result before running a command.  Run commands from the repository root. Use a new output directory for every run.  Keep the command, seed, and result—including failures.  Answer the chapter check before moving on.   Reading and exercise durations are planning estimates, not training-time guarantees. The first launch may download assets, compile kernels, and populate rendering caches.

title: Prepare your environment
text:
Runtime requirements  The reference environment is Ubuntu 24.04 on DGX Spark (aarch64), Python 3.12, Isaac Sim 6.2, and pinned Isaac Lab / Newton revisions. Simulation uses Newton’s native actuator path. Other GPUs or versions may run, but the course results do not automatically apply to them.  You need an NVIDIA driver, a GPU-enabled graphical desktop, Git, Docker, and network access to NVIDIA package sources. None of these are required for reading the website. Review the Isaac Sim license before installing the simulator.    Download the course and models    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    mkdir -p "$HOME/microduck"
cd "$HOME/microduck"
git clone https://github.com/NV-DLI/Microduck-Workshop.git
cd Microduck-Workshop
python3 scripts/workshop.py verify-models    The models are included in the repository, so no Hugging Face login is required. The verification command checks every model’s SHA-256. Continue only when all files match. Course weights and student outputs are stored separately.    Workspace  Copy command    Microduck-Workshop/
├── web/          # HTML course
├── lab/          # simulation and learning code
├── models/       # fixed course models
├── scripts/      # lab entry points
└── outputs/      # your runs (created when needed)      Prepare the simulator  First prepare system tools. The commands below install Git, Python virtual-environment support, and video encoding. Set up Docker using its  Ubuntu instructions ;  docker info  should show server information without a permission error.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    sudo apt-get update
sudo apt-get install -y git python3-venv ffmpeg
docker info
export UV_HTTP_TIMEOUT=600      Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py setup
python3 scripts/workshop.py doctor     setup  prepares the pinned runtime. If you already have a matching Isaac Lab checkout, bind it using  --isaaclab /path/to/IsaacLab .  doctor  checks Python, models, GPU, rendering, and navigation dependencies. Resolve failed checks before continuing.   Launch from your desktop terminal  Run GUI commands in a terminal on the GPU machine’s desktop. The website provides lessons and commands; Isaac opens in its own window. On the first launch, allow shaders and assets to finish loading.     Before you continue    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py inspect-model --model models/walk.onnx    Expected result: input and output names, tensor shapes, and model identity. If the GPU is unavailable, use the troubleshooting page before proceeding. Keep the pinned physics backend and model combination.

title: Meet Microduck’s mechanism
text: From assembly to components  Microduck is a small biped. Its legs support and move the body, the neck directs its view, and the trunk houses computing, power, and connections. Visual meshes describe appearance. Joints and collision geometry describe permitted motion and contact. These play different roles in simulation.       Open interactive model    Assembled   Exploded  Reset  Focus part    Rotate, zoom, and select a component  Drag to orbit and scroll to zoom, or use the component list below.   Select component   —     Try this: move the explosion slider halfway and find the leg servos. Fully expand the assembly and select the lens, shells, and boards. Reset the view and trace how the connectors form a kinematic chain.   Hardware revision and simulation joints  This CAD assembly contains 15 servo bodies. Its simulation export exposes 14 active joints; the beak is not an independent policy joint. Electronic shapes belong to the source CAD revision. Chapter 5 separately describes the Beta sensing configuration.      Play demonstration   Blender mechanical assembly illustration: components separate and reassemble. This explains structure; it is not a physics simulation.     Parts, joints, and degrees of freedom  A pen held at its tip can rotate in several directions, while a hinge normally rotates around one fixed axis. Robot joints impose similar constraints. A degree of freedom is an independent variable needed to describe permitted motion; a component count describes physical pieces. The 70 components in this viewer do not imply 70 policy actions.      Region  Active joints  Main role      Each leg  Hip yaw, roll, pitch; knee; ankle: 5 joints  Support the body and place the foot    Neck and head  Neck pitch; head pitch, yaw, roll: 4 joints  Orient the camera and head    Beak  Physical servo; not controlled by this policy  Shown in CAD, excluded from the 14-action interface      Select a hip servo and inspect its output shaft and nearby bearing. The servo controls an active angle, the bearing supports rotation, and brackets connect adjacent joints. Material, shape, and assembly clearance affect motion. The viewer preserves CAD detail but does not simulate screw preload, plastic elasticity, or cable forces; it is an anatomy aid rather than manufacturing documentation.    How software moves the mechanism    1 Policy action   2 Joint targets   3 Actuator torque   4 Physics update   5 New observation   A policy does not teleport the robot to a desired position. It outputs actions that become joint targets. Actuators produce torque based on the difference between target and measured state. The resulting motion depends on contact, gravity, inertia, and friction.  The policy runs at 50 Hz and physics at 200 Hz: each action spans four physics steps. Backlash introduces passive joints representing transmission play. Passive joints are not additional policy outputs.    Describe motion with frames      Frame  What is expressed here      World  Pitch, goal, and overall robot position    Body  Forward, lateral, and turn commands; ball relative to the robot    Camera  Image rays and detected target directions    Joint-local  A joint’s axis and angle       Check your understanding  If the head joints stay fixed, is the camera image necessarily stable?   Show explanation  No. Body pitch and roll move the neck and camera. Image stability depends on camera orientation relative to the world, not only on joint angles.      Exercise: trace one load path  Start with the assembled model. Trace a path from the left foot through the ankle, shin, knee, thigh, and hip. Ground support reaches the body through this chain. Explode the assembly and select the servos and brackets around a joint. Identify the fixed housing and the part driven by its output. Explosion offsets are display positions, not physically reachable joint poses.  A servo combines a motor, reduction gears, position feedback, and control electronics. Reaching a target takes time and is limited by torque, speed, friction, and backlash. A policy issuing an angle does not mean the joint instantly reaches it. Chapter 2 observes this difference; Chapter 3 explains how a policy learns around it.   Check your understanding  Does moving the foot farther out in the exploded view change the simulated leg length?   Show explanation  No. The web view explains components. Robot description files define simulated dimensions and joint connections.

title: Run your first simulation
text:
Before the lab     Play demonstration   Walking and re-observation within a full task, synchronized at simulation-time speed. Identify body motion and camera-view changes. The simpler walking command in this chapter does not include these perception and recovery states.   Complete setup and model verification. Open a desktop terminal on the GPU machine and enter  Microduck-Workshop . This chapter loads an existing model and focuses on a run’s inputs, outputs, and visible behavior.    What the policy receives and produces  This chapter runs inference with a trained policy. It maps the current observation to 14 joint actions without updating neural-network parameters. Changing the velocity command tests the same model under a different request; it is not training. Choosing a different model file changes the policy.      Observation, in interface order  Width  What it tells the policy      Angular velocity and projected gravity  6  Body rotation and tilt    Relative joint positions  14  Pose relative to the nominal posture    Joint velocities  14  Motion at each joint    Previous action  14  Previous control output and temporal context    Velocity, head, and body commands  3 + 4 + 6  Requested behavior      These values total 61. Reordering joints breaks their meaning even if the input still has 61 entries: the policy might read a knee as a hip. Course entry points preserve ordering, nominal posture, and control timing. Begin by changing commands, duration, and output directories; modify observation construction only after understanding the interface.    Load the fixed walking policy    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py walk \
  --model models/walk.onnx \
  --velocity 0.30 0.00 0.00 \
  --seconds 12 \
  --seed 42 \
  --output outputs/walk-forward-01        Argument  Meaning       --model   Explicit ONNX policy file     --velocity   Forward, lateral, and turn policy commands—not measured velocity     --seconds   Simulation duration     --seed   Random seed     --output   A new directory for this run      Expected result: a separate simulation window opens with the fixed policy controlling the robot. Watch alternating support, persistent body rotation, and drift around stopping. Use a new output directory for each observation.    Compare two commands    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py walk \
  --model models/walk.onnx \
  --velocity 0.00 0.00 0.00 \
  --seconds 12 \
  --seed 42 \
  --output outputs/walk-hold-01    Keep the model, duration, and seed unchanged, and set the command to zero. A zero command requests standing, but does not guarantee a perfectly motionless body. Small commands may not produce proportionally small motion; learned responses must be observed.   Check your understanding  Does changing the forward command from 0.30 to 0.15 guarantee exactly half the walking speed?   Show explanation  No. A command is an input; achieved speed is an outcome. Measure displacement and time under comparable conditions, including falls, unwanted turning, and command dead zones.      Read the outputs of one run  Physics advances every 0.005 seconds. The policy produces an action every 0.02 seconds, so four physics steps occur before the next policy update. Display refresh, physics frequency, and policy frequency are different quantities: a slow window does not automatically change simulated time.  The lab holds a zero velocity command for two seconds, then applies your command. After the run,  report.json  records elapsed simulation time, model identity, and whether a fall occurred.  trajectory.json  records positions and measured velocities over time. A fall ends the run instead of silently resetting it. This nominal single-robot observation does not replace the full perception-and-recovery task in Chapter 7.  Compare  fell  first, then displacement and measured velocity. Command entries are forward body velocity, lateral body velocity, and yaw rate. Units are meters, meters per second, and radians per second. Keep the seed fixed and change one parameter at a time so you can interpret the difference.   Check your understanding  The command is 0.30 m/s and measured speed averages 0.20 m/s without a fall. Is velocity tracking perfect?   Show explanation  No. Survival describes stability; velocity error describes tracking. Record them separately.

title: Learning to walk
text:
One reinforcement-learning loop     Play demonstration   Recorded parallel reinforcement learning: this basketball-balance run illustrates multi-environment sampling. It is not the walking exercise result or evidence of a successful basketball skill.   The policy receives a vector containing body attitude, angular velocity, joint state, a velocity command, and the previous action. It outputs joint actions, physics advances, and rewards measure progress toward the objective. PPO collects a batch of interactions, updates the policy, and samples again.    1 Observe   2 Sample actions   3 Simulate   4 Compute rewards   5 Update PPO   The environment count is the number of simultaneous robot copies. Iterations repeat collection and optimization. More environments increase parallel sampling and memory demand. A rising training reward means the optimized objective is improving; independent behavior checks are still necessary.    Why PPO looks beyond immediate reward  Lifting a foot can briefly reduce stability while being necessary for forward progress. Reinforcement learning therefore considers return over time rather than just the current reward. A discount factor reduces the weight of more distant rewards, balancing immediate feedback with longer-term consequences.  In PPO, the actor chooses actions and the critic estimates future return. An outcome better than the critic expected receives a positive advantage estimate, encouraging a higher probability for the corresponding action; a worse outcome does the opposite. PPO limits how far an update moves from the old policy to reduce abrupt changes. It does not guarantee that every update improves real task success.  A critic may receive additional simulation information to evaluate trajectories, but the deployed actor must depend only on observations available at runtime. A simulator knowing exact body velocity does not imply that hardware has a perfect velocity sensor. Keep training or scoring ground truth out of the deployed controller.  When designing rewards, list desired behaviors and then consider shortcuts. Rewarding ball motion may encourage body collisions; rewarding stillness may discourage walking. Track both goals and constraints: velocity error, episode length, falls, joint limits, and contact type. This chapter practices the training loop; Chapter 7 tests the complete task definition.    Run a short training exercise    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py train-walk \
  --num-envs 64 \
  --iterations 20 \
  --seed 101 \
  --output outputs/student-walk-01    This is a workflow exercise, not a promise that 20 iterations will learn to walk. Expected result: terminal progress, a new run directory, checkpoints, and an exported policy. Observe loss, return, and episode length without committing to a long training run.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py tensorboard \
  --logdir outputs/student-walk-01 \
  --port 6006    Open the local TensorBoard address printed in the terminal. Compare reward with episode length. If reward grows while episodes remain short, consider whether the objective rewards a brief action followed by a fall.    Explicitly test your own policy    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py walk \
  --model outputs/student-walk-01/exported/policy.onnx \
  --velocity 0.30 0.00 0.00 \
  --seconds 12 \
  --seed 202 \
  --output outputs/student-walk-test-01    Here you deliberately select your own model. Compare support, drift, and falls with the fixed model from Chapter 2. Later lessons still use  models/walk.onnx ; this export does not change their default.   Go further  To increase the budget, choose a new output directory and try, for example, 1,024 environments and 500 iterations. Check available memory and time first. A saved checkpoint is not a qualification result. Evaluate unseen seeds and retain failures.     Why domain randomization matters  Real actuators do not have identical friction, delay, and backlash on every run. Varying parameters in training exposes the policy to more conditions. A narrow range can overfit; an excessively broad range can make learning difficult. Randomization can improve robustness but does not replace hardware testing.   Check your understanding  Why is the highest-reward training episode not an independent test?   Show explanation  It contributed to learning or selection, and reward may differ from task success. Independent testing uses predetermined scenarios and success criteria and counts every outcome.      Checkpoints, curves, and independent tests  Practice starts from random parameters rather than the course walking weights. Each PPO iteration gathers trajectories from several environments and then updates the policy. Rewards combine velocity tracking, body attitude, action smoothness, and contact-related terms. Two policies with similar total rewards may obtain them through accurate motion or simply moving less; inspect both behavior and individual reward terms.   initial.pt  records initialization;  model_*.pt  files are checkpoints;  env.yaml  and  agent.yaml  preserve environment and optimizer settings;  exported/policy.onnx  is the inference export. A checkpoint can contain optimizer state, while ONNX normally preserves the inference graph. They are not interchangeable file formats.  Record the training budget, held-out test seeds, and observed behavior. The 20-iteration exercise teaches sampling, updates, saving, and export. A weak practice policy is no reason to replace downstream course defaults. For a larger budget, keep the earlier run, use a new output directory, and state whether you changed environment count, iteration count, or rewards.   Check your understanding  Does saving only ONNX guarantee an exact training continuation?   Show explanation  No. Exact continuation also needs optimizer, normalization and random states, together with matching configuration. Preserve full checkpoints and training settings.

title: From actions to complete skills
text:
Define a skill’s boundaries  Walking continuously accepts velocity commands. A kick is a short skill with a start and an end. Integrating it into an autonomous task requires entry conditions, a defined exit state, and a way to stop when conditions are unsafe.      Phase  What to check      Prepare  Ball in the kick region, acceptable heading, and fresh observations    Contact  Real foot contact moves the ball; ball state is not overwritten    Withdraw  End the kick and return to support    Recover  Remain stable without falling or exceeding joint limits        Understand a teacher and a residual  The course kick combines a fixed base policy with a trained residual model. The residual adjusts the base behavior, so observations, action scale, actuators, and timing must match. Removing one model does not leave an equivalent skill.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py inspect-model --model models/kick-teacher.onnx
python3 scripts/workshop.py inspect-model --model models/kick-residual.onnx    Find both files in the model inventory. Compare their input and output shapes and distinguish robot-state inputs from task inputs. The complete task uses the pair in Chapter 7; retraining is not required here.    Why ONNX files are not interchangeable  ONNX is a model representation, not a universal robot-skill protocol. The walking model takes 61 inputs, while the kicking residual takes 62. Both output 14 numbers, yet they are not interchangeable. Input ordering, additional state, action scaling, teacher blending, and termination conditions are all part of the runtime contract.  After inspecting the models, record their input and output shapes. Explain why successfully loading a file only proves that its format is readable, not that the robot will perform a skill. A valid file can still receive the wrong units or joint order. The fixed task entry point uses weights together with their required conventions.  Watch the kick in three phases: before it, inspect ball and support-foot positions; during it, identify whether contact comes from the foot or another body part; afterwards, inspect recovery of support. Pause the GIF in each phase and describe the entry and completion conditions. This is more informative than asking only whether the ball moved.    Watch contact and recovery     Play demonstration   Fixed-model example: the robot reobserves and approaches, then kicks and recovers. Focus on when a kick is permitted and what happens afterward.    Check your understanding  The ball enters the goal, but the robot falls afterward. Is the full skill successful?   Show explanation  Not under this course’s criteria. Success includes physical contact, a goal, and recovery. Checking ball position alone misses stability and motion limits.      Optional observation: balancing on a ball     Play demonstration   Parallel ball-balancing training illustrates exploration and reward feedback. This is training footage, not evidence of a reliable balancing skill, and it is not required for shooting.   Propose success criteria for balancing: duration, allowable body tilt, and whether ball motion is permitted. Finishing a training process is a program state; learning the skill requires a separate evaluation.    Describe a skill by its contract  Describe a skill using entry conditions, observations, actions, and exit conditions. A kick requires a useful right-foot ball position, goal alignment, stable support, and fresh target information. Execution combines the kicking teacher with a residual correction. It must then return to a stable standing or walking state; touching the ball alone does not finish the task.  A residual adds a constrained correction to an existing action. This reduces what must be learned from scratch but inherits the teacher’s operating range. Starting a local kick far from the ball does not make it search or approach. Navigation creates a valid handoff state; the skill performs its local action.   Check your understanding  The robot is beside the ball, but its remembered position has expired. Should the kick start immediately?   Show explanation  No. Observe again and confirm the entry conditions. Proximity alone does not guarantee valid inputs.

title: Seeing the football
text:
Three complementary sources      Source  Information  Limit      RGB  Image target location  No direct absolute range    ToF  64 forward range zones  Invalid zones are not free space    Body IMU  Attitude and angular velocity  Does not locate the ball or goal      The RGB detector finds image regions resembling a ball. ToF measures ranges across an 8 × 8 forward-facing grid; it is not a 360-degree lidar. A body IMU estimates attitude so image rays and ranges can be interpreted in the right frame. No single sensor supplies the complete world state.  The Beta simulation uses GC2093 camera and VL53L8CX ToF profiles. Images are processed at 960 × 540 and 15 Hz. Lens field of view and noise settings are simulation assumptions; physical devices require calibration.    Run the fixed detector first     Play demonstration   Actual fixed-detector outputs on eight different sample images, one image per second. These are separate static samples, not a continuous camera video or inference-speed measurement.     Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py detect \
  --model models/detector.pt \
  --source datasets/sample/images \
  --output outputs/detection-01    Expected result: images with ball and goal detections. Inspect small targets, image boundaries, and occlusion. Confidence is a model score, not a guarantee that a detection is correct.    1 RGB image   2 Detection box   3 Image ray   4 Range and ground constraints   5 Target in the body frame     Practice training a detector    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py train-detector \
  --data datasets/sample/data.yaml \
  --epochs 5 \
  --batch 8 \
  --seed 303 \
  --output outputs/student-detector-01    The small dataset and five epochs introduce data, labels, training, and validation; this is not a full training recipe. Inspect loss curves and validation images. To improve quality, diversify scenes and keep training, validation, and test scenes separate.   Keep the course detector downstream  Chapters 6 and 7 use  models/detector.pt  by default. The practice model does not replace it. Detection mAP measures detection quality, not shooting success.     From a pixel to a spatial ray  Let a detection center be pixel (u, v), with camera focal lengths (fx, fy) and principal point (cx, cy). In a common camera convention, the viewing ray is proportional to ((u−cx)/fx, (v−cy)/fy, 1). This gives direction but cannot distinguish a small nearby object from a larger distant one. Range or a known geometric constraint is still needed.  Camera coordinates commonly use x right, y down, z forward. Here the body convention is x forward, y left, z up. Transform using the camera’s rotation and translation relative to the body rather than mixing same-named axes. Head motion changes this transform, so localization requires joint state at the appropriate time.  An 8 × 8 ToF grid does not provide 64 independent object labels. One cell may cover both floor and ball, and close reflections may be invalid. Check measurement status and range before associating a return with an image target. Treating an invalid reading as an obstacle-free direction gives navigation a false premise.    A past observation can become stale  After moving or tilting its head, the robot may lose the ball from view. Odometry can update a remembered relative position briefly, but error accumulates. Stale observations, invalid ranges, or lost ground constraints require stopping and reobserving. Missing data is not free space.   Check your understanding  If a ball box is accurate, can its center be used directly as a world coordinate?   Show explanation  No. Pixels give an image direction. Spatial position also requires a camera model, camera pose, and distance or geometric constraints.      Inspect labels and detections  The sample has 40 images split into 24 training, 8 validation, and 8 test images. Class 0 is the ball and class 1 the goal. Each YOLO label row is  class cx cy width height , with the last four values normalized by image dimensions. A horizontal center of 0.5 means halfway across the image, not 0.5 meters in the world.  Choose one clear prediction and one difficult example. Check missed objects, false detections, and misplaced boxes, then compare object size and position. High confidence cannot repair camera calibration or turn a 2D box into depth. Navigation still requires range, attitude, timestamps, and validity checks.   Check your understanding  Can a ball label centered at (0.6, 0.4) be used directly as a navigation target at (0.6 m, 0.4 m)?   Show explanation  No. These are normalized image coordinates. A camera model and range or ground constraint are needed to obtain robot-relative position.

title: Navigate to a useful kicking position
text:
The ball center is not the destination  Walking straight toward the ball center can cause premature contact or approach from the wrong side. A useful target lies behind the ball. The ball-to-goal direction defines the shooting axis; move backward along it and account for the kicking foot’s lateral offset.   A planar geometry exercise  Direction  d = (goal − ball) / ‖goal − ball‖  Target  target = ball − distance × d + lateral × normal(d)      Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py plan \
  --ball 0.00 -0.02 \
  --goal 0.93 0.00 \
  --distance 0.18 \
  --lateral 0.035 \
  --output outputs/plan-01    Expected result: a target position, heading, and a planar diagram. Change the ball’s lateral coordinate and observe how the target moves. This exercise uses known 2D points to teach geometry; autonomous execution uses sensor estimates.    How path planning and walking divide the work  A planner searches for a route through a representation of space. An occupancy grid divides the floor into cells for obstacles, free space, and unknown space. A robot has a footprint: it cannot pass through every gap that admits a mathematical point. Reserving clearance is necessary when turning a geometric route into executable motion.  Nav2 provides CPU navigation services in the full task, while the walking policy maintains bipedal balance. The upper layer requests a target or velocity; the lower layer drives servos. Actuator delay and gait error can move the robot away from its plan, so the system must observe and reconsider instead of assuming exact command execution.  The hand-calculation exercise studies stance geometry only: it does not call Nav2 or place obstacles. The full task uses one robot, ball, and goal in an empty field. Adding obstacles requires new checks for sensor coverage, unknown space, clearance, and collisions. Empty-field results do not establish obstacle-avoidance performance.    Approach in stages    1 Search and observe   2 Coarse approach   3 Fine alignment   4 Check kick conditions   5 Kick and recover   At a distance, reducing range is the main priority. Nearby, motion must become more precise while preserving visibility, heading, and foot placement. Being close enough is not sufficient if heading is wrong.  A planner supplies a route or direction; the walking policy executes it. A valid planned path does not prove the robot has traversed it. The system must handle tracking errors, contact, and sensor updates.    Reobserve when information is lost     Play demonstration   Watch the retreat, reobservation, and renewed approach. Retreat restores observation and maneuvering space rather than immediately reducing target distance.    Check your understanding  ToF becomes invalid during approach, but the remembered ball position looks plausible. Should the robot continue forward?   Show explanation  Not merely because it looks plausible. Check memory age and current ground, range, and attitude information. Stop and reobserve when the required conditions are absent.      Work through a stance target  Subtract the ball position from the goal center and normalize the result to obtain the shooting direction. The stance lies behind the ball: move back by  distance  along that direction, then sideways by  lateral  to allow space for the kicking leg. This exercise defines its own offset convention; it does not replace calibrated entry values in the physical skill.  Open  plan.svg  to inspect the stance, ball, and goal.  plan.json  gives the target position and heading. Change distance from 0.18 to 0.25 with a new output directory; predict the direction of movement and check it. This command computes geometry from known points. It runs no physics and does not prove reachability.  The full task also handles yaw drift, delayed gait response, and targets leaving view at close range. Approach therefore updates observations and checks stopping conditions repeatedly. If valid range or floor support is lost, stop or retreat within constraints and observe again. Unknown space cannot be declared free space.

title: Complete the autonomous task
text:
Understand the complete system  This is not a single network issuing a “score” command. A walking policy controls the body, a detector supplies visual targets, range and attitude constrain relative position, a state machine decides when to observe, walk, and kick, and the kick models execute contact and recovery.    1 RGB + ToF + IMU   2 Target estimates   3 Navigate and align   4 Fixed kick models   5 Task evaluation      Play demonstration   A complete successful autonomous kick, synchronized robot and external views at simulation-time speed. A single example is not an independent success-rate measurement.     Run the complete teaching scene    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py football \
  --seed 983102 \
  --seconds 180 \
  --output outputs/football-01    Expected result: an Isaac simulation window opens and one robot searches, approaches, aligns, and attempts a kick autonomously. The program uses the repository’s fixed models and saves video, traces, and results. The 180-second budget is simulation time, not wall-clock waiting time. Initialization and rendering can take longer.  This seed is a selected teaching fixture drawn from successful examples. It supports comparison on the same scene and is not a new independent success-rate sample. Do not manually move the robot or ball during execution. To stop, press Ctrl+C in the terminal and retain the logs.    Judge complete success    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py report --run outputs/football-01     A real foot–ball contact occurred.  The entire ball crossed the goal plane inside the opening.  The robot did not fall or exceed the specified mechanical bounds.  There was no premature ball contact, and the robot recovered after kicking.    Interpreting the reference result  The fixed combination completed 9 of 10 independent empty-field episodes. This is a small-sample observation for specific versions and a scene distribution, not a guarantee for arbitrary seeds, obstacles, or hardware. Obstacles and real-robot deployment are outside the validated main path.     Design a small evaluation  Write down seeds and success criteria before running. Record goals, falls, contact, and recovery for every episode. Do not replace a failure with a retry. A model or parameter change defines a separate experiment.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py football \
  --seed 990001 \
  --seconds 180 \
  --output outputs/football-new-seed-01     Check your understanding  Why can the task fail even when detection mAP is high and the walking policy stays upright?   Show explanation  Success depends on interfaces between modules. Targets can leave view, coordinates or observation age can become unsuitable, and position or heading may fail the kick conditions. Module metrics do not replace end-to-end evaluation.      Capstone: produce a reviewable result  Run the default teaching case and retain the complete output. Submit a short account of model origin, seed, time budget, final outcome, and observations from both views. If it fails, preserve the directory and identify the perception, approach, contact, scoring, or recovery stage. Do not repeatedly rerun and submit only the best attempt.  With additional compute time, declare five new seeds in advance, for example 990001–990005. Use identical fixed models, a 180-second budget, and separate output directories, running sequentially. Record all five outcomes, including missed goals and execution errors. Report errors separately with their causes rather than silently deleting them. Five trials remain a small experiment with substantial statistical uncertainty.      Field  Example or requirement      Models  Fixed course models; retain identity checks    Parameters  Seed, seconds, output directory    Behavior  Contact, whole-ball crossing, fall, recovery    Evidence  result.json, traces, complete synchronized video    Interpretation  One observed phenomenon and its supporting evidence      Completion means running the system, explaining its parts, and assessing results honestly. It does not require a short personal training run to match all course performance. You now know how to preserve a working model, try new training without damaging a baseline, and distinguish local metrics from task success. Hardware work additionally requires independent sensor calibration, actuator-limit checks, and control-interface validation.    What you have connected  Starting from the mechanism, you connected joint control, reinforcement learning, vision, range and attitude estimation, navigation, and a short motion skill. In further experiments, change one clear factor at a time and preserve the mapping between models, environments, and results.    Locate a problem from a failed run  First check whether  result.json  was produced. If not, inspect the terminal error and installation or runtime conditions: that is an execution failure. If results exist, distinguish failure to find the ball, failure to reach a kicking stance, contact without a goal, and failure to recover after scoring. A normal process exit does not mean the robot completed the task.   course_evaluation.passed  combines physical scoring and applicable checks.  scorer  retains contact, goal crossing, and fall information. In synchronized views, inspect the stance before first contact and posture after kicking. A short clip of the ball crossing the line is insufficient for a full-task judgment.  The fixed combination completed 9/10 recorded independent empty-field trials under a particular environment, distribution, and time budget. The default seed 983102 is a teaching example; repeating it does not establish a new independent success rate. New seeds, different devices, obstacles, and real hardware require separate evaluation.

title: Models and data
text: Course model inventory      File  Purpose       walk.onnx   Fixed walking policy     kick-teacher.onnx   Base kicking action     kick-residual.onnx   Residual kick adjustment     kick-checkpoint.pt   Retained kick training checkpoint     detector.pt   Fixed visual detector     detector.onnx   ONNX detector export        Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py verify-models    These files are included in Git without Git LFS or a separate model account.  models/manifest.json  records sizes, sources, and SHA-256 identities. Model identity checks guard against accidental same-name replacements.    Practice data and your outputs   datasets/sample/  is a small image-and-label practice set for detector inference and short training. It is not enough to establish real-world generalization. Student checkpoints and logs belong in  outputs/ ; do not copy them over the course files in  models/ .    Sources and usage terms  Robot geometry, community policies, and dependencies retain their source terms. The course-code license does not override third-party asset licenses. Before redistributing changes, read the repository’s  attribution and license notices .

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Start with the environment report    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py doctor
python3 scripts/workshop.py verify-models    The first failure is more useful than repeatedly launching a full training run. Check the repository directory, the selected runtime, and all model checks.    Common issues      Symptom  What to check      No GUI window  Use the GPU desktop terminal and check DISPLAY and the driver. A remote text shell is not a graphical desktop.    First launch is slow  Check for downloads and compilation. Allow initialization and avoid starting duplicate instances.    Output directory exists  Choose a new run name and preserve the previous result.    Out of memory  Reduce training environments or detector batch size. Avoid concurrent simulations.    Model hash mismatch  Restore the repository model and check for accidental overwrites.    Practice policy walks poorly  A short run teaches the workflow. Inspect reward, episode length, and evaluation. Continue with fixed models.    Robot stops or does not score  Inspect the task report and observation validity. Stopping can be appropriate when information is missing; it is not a goal.        Inspect a run    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py report --run outputs/football-01    When reporting an issue, include the command, seed, environment report, and first error. A success/failure label alone is not enough. Do not include passwords or access tokens.

title: Further learning and references
text: Robotics and simulation  Begin with task observations, actions, and rewards, then explore physics and sensors. Course commands target fixed versions; current documentation may describe newer versions. Check the version before applying changes.    Suggested extensions   Vary the Chapter 3 training budget and compare on the same unseen seeds.  Add backgrounds and lighting conditions to Chapter 5 and evaluate generalization.  Visualize Chapter 6 target positions and headings for different ball locations.  Predefine new seeds for Chapter 7 and retain all successes and failures.
